lessons.unit: Autumn 1: Transition to Key Stage 4: study habits, revision and wellbeing
lessons.title: Managing stress and exam pressure
lessons.bigQuestion: You have about 52 teaching weeks before your International GCSE exams. Is that a long time or a short time?
objectives: To understand how to manage the pressure of a two-year GCSE course with effective study habits and wellbeing strategies
successCriteria: All: name signs of exam stress and three coping strategies
Most: plan a weekly study routine with spaced retrieval practice
Some: explain why retrieval and spacing beat re-reading, and when to seek help
lessons.crossCurricular: All International GCSE subjects: revision techniques

keywords.def: recalling information from memory to strengthen it
revisiting topics over days and weeks
the body's response to pressure
feeling healthy and able to cope

hook.text: You have about 52 teaching weeks before your International GCSE exams. Is that a long time or a short time?
hook.a: Both: enough with steady habits from now; too short if left to the end.

islamicLink.text: Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity (al-Baqarah 2:286). The Prophet ﷺ said that the most beloved deeds to Allah are those done regularly, even if small (al-Bukhari and Muslim): steady daily study beats last-minute cramming.

starter.q: Which is better for memory? A) re-reading notes B) testing yourself
How much sleep do teenagers need?
Name one exam you will sit in 2028.

teach.heading: The course ahead
teach.note: Founding year: content is front-loaded; an extra hour of independent study per subject per week.

teach.heading: Study that works
bullets: Spacing: revisit after 1 day, 1 week, 1 month
teach.note: Re-reading and highlighting feel productive but are weaker.

teach.heading: Managing stress
bullets: Break work into blocks (25 minutes on, 5 off)
teach.note: Model a weekly plan.

model.problem: Plan a weekday evening for a Year 10 pupil.
steps: Two 25-minute blocks: maths retrieval, science flashcards
model.answer: Balanced evening with spaced retrieval and rest

teach.heading: When to get help
bullets: Stress stops sleep, eating or learning
teach.note: Safeguarding: any thoughts of self-harm: tell someone today.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: Which revision method is best supported by evidence?
check.why: Retrieval and spacing strengthen memory; the others feel easy but help less.

practice.q: Turn a page of notes into five flashcard questions.
practice.model: Teacher turns a science paragraph into two flashcards.

independent.q: Core: Weekly study plan (pupil PDF): subjects, retrieval blocks, breaks, prayer, exercise and sleep.
independent.a: A realistic weekly plan with spacing.

independent.q: Extend: In the portal response box, describe your warning signs of stress and your plan. Start: 'When I notice...'
independent.a: When I notice I'm not sleeping, I will reduce screen time, talk to my parents and use my plan.

exit.q: Spaced practice means... A) cramming the night before B) revisiting topics over days and weeks C) never revising
exit.a: B) revisiting topics over days and weeks

exit.q: Big question: is 52 weeks a long time? What will you do this week?
exit.a: Enough with steady habits; for example, two retrieval blocks a day.

lessons.homework: Follow your study plan for one week and tick each block.
lessons.send: SEND: a plan with blocks pre-drawn. EAL: retrieval, spacing glossary. Stretch: research the 'forgetting curve'.

lessons.title: Healthy relationships, marriage and the law
objectives: Describe features of a healthy, committed relationship and the Islamic view of marriage
Explain that consent is essential in marriage and that forced marriage is illegal
Recognise domestic abuse and coercive control and know where to find help

keywords.def: a legal and spiritual contract between two consenting adults
a marriage without the full and free consent of both people
a pattern of behaviour that dominates and isolates a person
abusive behaviour by a family member, spouse or partner
love and mercy, as in Qur'an 30:21

starter: Name two signs of an unhealthy relationship.
Name one helpline for young people.

teach.heading: What makes a healthy committed relationship?
teach.note: Say bismillah. Teach in line with the TGA RSHE Policy, to boys and girls separately; parents have been informed and can see all materials. TGA pupils live in different countries: use UK law as the baseline and remind pupils that laws vary elsewhere. Cite plainly: Qur'an 30:21, that Allah placed love and mercy between spouses. Cite the hadith that the best of you are the best to your families (Tirmidhi). Link to the Tarbiyyah Compass values of Integrity and Excellence. Ground rules: right to pass, no personal stories, kindness. Anonymous questions can go to the teacher's question box. If a pupil says anything that worries you, stay calm, do not promise secrecy and follow the Child Protection and Safeguarding Policy: tell the DSL the same day.

teach.heading: Marriage in Islam
bullets: Marriage is a contract based on consent
Hadith: a woman must be consulted and give permission
Parents advise and support; they do not force
teach.note: Cite plainly: the Prophet (peace be upon him) said that a previously married woman must not be married until she is consulted, and a virgin must not be married until her permission is sought (Bukhari and Muslim). Teach that Islam requires free consent. Explain that families can guide with wisdom, but forcing is not permitted. Misconception: forced marriage is a religious or cultural duty. It is not.

teach.heading: The law and forced marriage
bullets: Forced marriage is a crime in England and Wales
The minimum age to marry is 18
teach.note: State clearly: since 2014 forcing someone to marry is a criminal offence in England and Wales, and since February 2023 the minimum age for marriage is 18, including for religious-only ceremonies. Explain that taking a child abroad to be married is also an offence. Pupils at risk can contact the Forced Marriage Unit, the DSL, Childline or the police. Reassure pupils that this is a protective law. If concerned about any pupil, follow safeguarding procedures the same day.

teach.heading: Domestic abuse and coercive control
bullets: Abuse can be physical, emotional, financial or online
Never the victim's fault and never acceptable
Hadith: do not harm or return harm
teach.note: Define domestic abuse and coercive control with invented examples: a partner controls money, checks messages and cuts someone off from family. Cite the hadith ‘There should be neither harming nor reciprocating harm’ (Ibn Majah; Nawawi's Forty Hadith no. 32) and Qur'an 4:19 on treating spouses with kindness. Explain that abuse is not justified by religion or culture. Do not ask pupils to share their own experiences.

teach.heading: Getting help
teach.note: Share the helplines and explain they are confidential. Explain what to say: ‘I am worried about my safety or someone else's.’ Mention that FGM is also illegal in the UK and that anyone concerned should tell the DSL or contact the police; keep this factual. Close with a reminder that the school will always listen and act. Follow safeguarding procedures immediately if a concern arises.

practice: True or false? (a) In England and Wales the minimum age for marriage is 16. (b) Both people must freely consent to a marriage in Islam. (c) Coercive control can include monitoring someone's phone.
List three features of a healthy marriage from the lesson.
Write what you could say to a friend who tells you they are afraid of being forced to marry.
independent: Write a short advice leaflet: ‘Healthy relationships and the law’ with four key facts and two helplines.
Create a case study showing coercive control and the steps taken to seek help.
Write a paragraph on how Qur'an 30:21 and the hadith on consent shape Islamic marriage.
exit: Give two features of a healthy relationship.
What does UK law say about forced marriage?
lessons.homework: Write down three qualities of a healthy relationship you would look for in the future, linked to Islamic teaching.
lessons.send: SEND: provide key facts on cards and a visual of helplines. EAL: pre-teach legal vocabulary. Stretch: compare how UK law and Islamic principles each protect individuals in marriage.

lessons.title: Gambling and risk: why it harms
lessons.bigQuestion: Betting adverts show winners. Why do gambling companies make billions if people keep winning?
objectives: To understand how gambling is designed to make people lose money, the harm it causes, and why Islam forbids it
successCriteria: All: define gambling and name forms of it, including in games
Most: explain the house edge and why gamblers lose over time
Some: explain the links between gaming loot boxes and gambling, and where to get help

keywords.def: risking money on an uncertain result to win more
gambling, forbidden in Islam (مَيْسِر)
the built-in advantage that makes the operator win over time
a paid random reward in a video game

hook.text: Betting adverts show winners. Why do gambling companies make billions if people keep winning?
hook.a: Because, over time, most people lose: the odds favour the operator.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'O you who believe, intoxicants, gambling (maysir), stone altars and divining arrows are defilement from the work of Satan, so avoid it that you may succeed' (al-Ma'idah 5:90), and that Satan wants to cause enmity through them and turn you from remembering Allah (5:91).

starter.q: Probability of rolling a 6 on a fair dice?

starter.a: Repeated behaviour causing alarm or distress.

starter.q: Legal age for most gambling in the UK?

teach.heading: What counts as gambling?
bullets: Some game features feel similar: loot boxes
teach.note: UK legal age for most gambling (including the National Lottery) is 18.

teach.heading: The house edge
teach.note: Model.

model.problem: A game: pay £1, 1 in 6 chance to win £5 (you keep the prize, not your £1). Expected result per go?
model.answer: You lose about 17p each go on average

teach.heading: The harm
teach.note: Signs: secrecy, borrowing, mood swings.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: Why do gambling operators make profit overall?
options: The odds give them an edge
check.why: The house edge means players lose on average over time.

practice.q: Pay £2 for a 1 in 10 chance of £15 (prize only). Expected loss per go?
practice.model: Teacher works expected value step by step.

independent.q: Core: Advert analysis (pupil PDF): identify three persuasion techniques in an invented betting advert and what it hides.
independent.a: Free bets, celebrity, 'win big'; hides losses and risks.

independent.q: Extend: In the portal response box, explain whether loot boxes are like gambling. Start: 'Loot boxes are similar because...'
independent.a: Similar: pay for a random reward; can encourage repeated spending; Muslims should avoid chance-based paid rewards.

independent.q: Stretch: Where can someone get help with gambling harm?
independent.a: Parents, GP, the National Gambling Helpline (GamCare).

exit.q: Maysir means... A) charity B) gambling, forbidden in Islam C) trade
Big question: why do companies make billions if adverts show winners?
exit.a: Most people lose over time because of the house edge.

lessons.homework: Count gambling adverts you see in one day (TV, online, sport shirts) and write how they try to persuade.
lessons.send: SEND: expected value worked frame. EAL: odds, edge, addiction. Stretch: research UK rules on gambling adverts.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Staying safe and preparing for work
lessons.title: World of work: CVs, work experience and employability
objectives: Write a clear CV and plan for work experience
Explain basic rights and responsibilities at work, including health and safety, with Islamic values of amanah and ihsan

keywords.def: skills that make you suitable for work, such as teamwork
a short document summarising your education, skills and experience
a short placement in a workplace
the lowest hourly pay an employer can legally offer
trustworthiness and responsibility

starter: Bismillah. Name two skills you have.
Name one job you would like to try.

teach.heading: Employability skills
teach.note: Say bismillah. Ask what employers want. Link each skill to evidence from school life: organising a charity event, leading a group project, keeping to deadlines. Cite plainly: the hadith in which the Prophet (peace be upon him) said that Allah has prescribed ihsan, excellence, in all things (Muslim). Link to the Tarbiyyah Compass values of Integrity and Excellence. Refer to the TGA Careers Education and Guidance Policy. Ground rules: right to pass, no personal stories, kindness. Anonymous questions can go to the teacher's question box. If a pupil says anything that worries you, stay calm, do not promise secrecy and follow the Child Protection and Safeguarding Policy: tell the DSL the same day.

teach.heading: Writing a CV
bullets: Contact details, profile, education, skills, experience
One page, clear headings, no spelling errors
Use evidence: ‘Led a team of 4 to raise £150’
teach.note: Show a model CV for an invented pupil, Aisha Rahman: profile sentence, GCSEs being studied, skills (Arabic, public speaking), responsibility (house captain), volunteering (food bank). Ask pupils to identify strengths. Misconception: you need paid experience; volunteering and school roles count. Remind pupils not to include sensitive personal information such as date of birth or home address online.

teach.heading: Work experience and interviews
bullets: Answer with STAR: Situation, Task, Action, Result
teach.note: Model a STAR answer: Situation: our class project was behind schedule. Task: I needed to organise the team. Action: I made a shared plan and checked progress. Result: we finished on time. Practise with a partner in breakout rooms. Discuss options for remote or local placements and prayer arrangements, which can be discussed politely with an employer. Mention that the careers lead can help to find placements.

teach.heading: Rights, pay and safety
bullets: Minimum wage depends on age (check gov.uk)
Under-18s have limits on hours and rest breaks
Employers must provide a safe workplace
teach.note: Explain that in April 2025 the minimum wage for under-18s was £7.55 an hour; teachers should check gov.uk for the current rate. Worked example: 6 hours at £7.55 = £45.30. Explain that employers must follow health and safety law and young workers must be supervised. Discuss reporting channels: supervisor, parent, school, ACAS or the Health and Safety Executive. Link to Qur'an 83:1-3 on fairness in dealings.

teach.heading: Work with halal values
bullets: Earn halal income by honest means
Hadith: best food is from the work of your hands (Bukhari)
teach.note: Cite plainly: the hadith that no one has eaten better food than that which he eats from the work of his own hands (Bukhari). Discuss how to remain true to values in a workplace: honesty, respect, polite negotiation for prayer breaks. Mention that the hadith of the truthful and trustworthy merchant is related by Tirmidhi. Close with a du'a for beneficial knowledge and halal provision.

practice: Turn this into a strong CV line: ‘I help in my mosque.’
Calculate pay: 5 hours at £7.55 an hour.
Write a STAR answer to: ‘Tell me about a time you worked in a team.’
independent: Write your first CV using the template: profile, education, skills, responsibilities and interests.
Write a letter asking a local business for work experience.
Write a paragraph on how amanah and ihsan help you at work.
lessons.homework: Complete your CV and ask a parent or carer to give one piece of feedback. Write what you changed.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a CV template and sentence starters. EAL: pre-teach CV vocabulary. Stretch: research one employer, prepare three interview questions and a STAR answer.

lessons.title: Respect and responsibility
lessons.bigQuestion: At 15 you have more freedom online. Does more freedom mean more responsibility?
objectives: To understand how respect and responsibility apply in the family, with friends and online, and what the law expects
successCriteria: All: describe respectful behaviour at home, with friends and online
Most: explain legal responsibilities online (harassment, sharing others' information)
Some: explain how Islamic adab and UK law together shape responsible behaviour
lessons.crossCurricular: Citizenship: criminal responsibility from age 10 in England and Wales

keywords.def: treating others as valuable
being accountable for our actions
good manners and conduct (أَدَب)
repeated behaviour that causes alarm or distress, a crime in the UK

hook.text: At 15 you have more freedom online. Does more freedom mean more responsibility?
hook.a: Yes: freedom and accountability grow together, in law and in Islam.

islamicLink.text: Allah commands kindness to parents (al-Isra 17:23-24) and justice even against ourselves (an-Nisa 4:135). The Prophet ﷺ said each of you is a shepherd and responsible for his flock (al-Bukhari and Muslim).

starter.q: Age of criminal responsibility in England and Wales?

starter.a: No screenshots of others; chat for learning.

teach.heading: Respect at home
bullets: Speaking well even when we disagree
teach.note: 17:23: not even saying 'uff' to parents.

teach.heading: Respect with friends and online
bullets: Do not share others' information or images
teach.note: Respect for every person, whatever their background or beliefs.

teach.heading: The law and responsibility
bullets: Harassment and threatening messages can be crimes
Sharing private images of under-18s is illegal
Data and privacy law protects personal information
teach.note: Factual, no detail beyond the law.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

options: Checking before sharing and refusing to spread gossip
check.why: Checking and refusing gossip follows both law and adab (49:6, 49:12).

practice.model: Teacher rewrites, separating the idea from the person.

independent.q: Core: Scenarios (pupil PDF): for five situations at home, with friends and online, write the respectful and responsible choice.
Extend: In the portal response box, explain how adab and UK law agree on online behaviour. Start: 'Both Islam and the law...'
independent.a: Both Islam and the law forbid harming others with words, spreading private information and harassment.

independent.q: Stretch: Explain the meaning of 'each of you is a shepherd' for a 15-year-old.
independent.a: We are responsible for our own conduct, siblings, and what we share.

exit.q: Harassment in the UK is... A) legal B) a crime C) only rude
Big question: does more freedom mean more responsibility? Why?
exit.a: Yes: we are accountable in law and before Allah for how we use it.

lessons.homework: Do one extra responsibility at home this week without being asked and note how it went.
lessons.send: SEND: scenario cards with choices. EAL: respect, responsibility, harassment. Stretch: research the Online Safety Act 2023.

lessons.title: Substances: harms, the law and getting help
lessons.bigQuestion: Is giving a friend an illegal drug for free 'supplying'?
objectives: To understand the effects of drugs and alcohol, how UK law classifies them, and how to get help
successCriteria: All: describe the short- and long-term harms of alcohol, cannabis and nitrous oxide
Most: explain the Misuse of Drugs Act classes and penalties
Some: explain how exploitation (county lines) uses young people, and where to get help
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: the nervous system and drugs
lessons.smsc: Moral: protecting the mind and body

keywords.def: the three legal classes of controlled drugs
having an illegal drug
giving or selling drugs, even to friends
gangs using young people to move drugs

hook.text: Is giving a friend an illegal drug for free 'supplying'?
hook.a: Yes: in UK law, giving drugs to someone, even free, counts as supply.

islamicLink.text: The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Every intoxicant is khamr and every khamr is forbidden' (Muslim). Allah says: 'Do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction' (al-Baqarah 2:195). Protecting the mind ('aql) is one of the aims of the Shari'ah.

starter.q: Expected value of most gambling for the player is...
Legal age to buy alcohol in the UK?

teach.heading: Effects
bullets: Cannabis: memory, mental health, psychosis risk
Nitrous oxide: nerve damage, B12 deficiency
teach.note: Factual and calm.

teach.heading: The law: Misuse of Drugs Act 1971
bullets: Class C: nitrous oxide (since 2023), some tranquillisers
teach.note: Maximum penalties.

teach.heading: County lines
bullets: Gangs recruit young people to move drugs
teach.note: Signs: unexplained money, new phones, missing from home. Tell the safeguarding lead.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.why: Cannabis is Class B in the UK.

practice.q: Maximum sentence for possession of a Class B drug?
practice.model: Teacher reads the table row and explains 'maximum'.

independent.q: Core: Case studies (pupil PDF, invented): identify the harm, the law and the help available.
independent.a: Correct harms, laws and help for each.

independent.q: Extend: In the portal response box, write advice to a younger sibling about a 'free gift' from an older stranger. Start: 'If someone...'
independent.a: If someone gives you gifts and then asks for favours, it may be grooming for county lines; tell a parent or teacher.

independent.q: Stretch: Explain why the law treats supply more seriously than possession.
independent.a: Supply spreads harm to others and fuels crime.

exit.q: Giving a friend drugs for free is... A) legal B) supply C) nothing
Big question: where could a young person get help with drugs or exploitation?
exit.a: Parents, safeguarding lead, GP, Talk to FRANK, Childline.

lessons.homework: Read the Talk to FRANK page on one drug with a parent and note two facts.
lessons.send: SEND: table printed with key facts highlighted. EAL: possession, supply, exploitation. Stretch: research the Psychoactive Substances Act 2016.

lessons.title: Online exploitation and grooming: spotting and reporting
lessons.bigQuestion: Someone online is always kind, gives you gifts and says 'only I understand you'. Is that friendship?
objectives: To understand how online grooming and exploitation work and how to report them
successCriteria: All: name warning signs of grooming
Most: explain the stages groomers use to build trust and control
Some: explain how to report to CEOP and why victims are never to blame
lessons.crossCurricular: Computing: privacy settings and online security

keywords.def: building trust with a young person in order to exploit them
using someone for another's gain
the National Crime Agency's child protection command, which takes reports online
controls over who sees and contacts you

hook.text: Someone online is always kind, gives you gifts and says 'only I understand you'. Is that friendship?
hook.a: It may be grooming: gifts, flattery and isolation are warning signs.

islamicLink.text: Islam commands protecting the vulnerable and forbids deception. Allah says: 'Cooperate in righteousness and piety, but do not cooperate in sin and aggression' (al-Ma'idah 5:2). Telling an adult about exploitation protects you and others.

starter.a: Gangs using young people to move drugs.
Private account, who can message me.
The staff member responsible for keeping pupils safe.

teach.heading: What is grooming?
bullets: Can be for crime, money or abuse
teach.note: Age-appropriate and non-graphic. Groomers can pretend to be young.

teach.heading: Common stages
teach.note: Recognise the pattern early.

teach.heading: Warning signs
bullets: Asks to move to a private app
teach.note: Never share images; if someone threatens, it is not your fault: tell someone.

teach.heading: Reporting
bullets: Tell a parent or the safeguarding lead
teach.note: Explain CEOP's online reporting button.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: An online contact says 'Keep our chats secret from your parents'. This is...
check.why: Isolation from trusted adults is a key grooming tactic.

practice.q: List three warning signs from the slides.
practice.a: Secrets, gifts, moving to a private app.
practice.model: Teacher lists one and explains why.

independent.q: Core: Chat analysis (pupil PDF, invented): highlight warning signs and write what the young person should do.
independent.a: Signs identified; stop, screenshot, block, tell, report.
independent.model: Teacher highlights the first warning sign.

independent.q: Extend: Check your own privacy settings on one app with a parent and record two changes.
Stretch: In the portal response box, explain why victims are never to blame. Start: 'Victims are never to blame because...'
independent.a: Victims are never to blame because groomers deliberately deceive and manipulate them.

exit.q: CEOP is... A) a game B) a place to report online child exploitation C) a social network
exit.a: B) a place to report online child exploitation
options: A place to report online exploitation

exit.q: Big question: kind, gifts, 'only I understand you': friendship or grooming?
exit.a: Possibly grooming: these are warning signs; tell a trusted adult.

lessons.homework: With a parent, review who can contact you on each app you use.
lessons.send: SEND: warning signs checklist. EAL: grooming, exploit, report. Stretch: research how the Online Safety Act 2023 protects children.
